newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet reshuffle may hamper privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet reshuffle may hamper privatisation.

text.p: Political bargaining between Poland's two ruling leftist parties over a coming cabinet reshuffle may temporarily hamper if not paralyse privatisation, Privatisation Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek said on Thursday.
Kaczmarek's protfolio is to be replaced by a more powerful treasury ministry as of October 1 under a cabinet reform and the two parties remain divided over who should head it.

Kaczmarek said that if the coalition fails to reach a compromise it may consider appointing a temporary, acting treasury minister, with no real powers, which would hit not only privatisation but also the way state assets were managed.

"It is now up to political elites, coalition's leadership, whether they want to take a risk and disturb the privatisation process and to take a decision which would help avoid such disturbance," he said.
"Appointing an acting minister from October 1 would be a conscious action...paralysing decision-making," he said.
By law, all senior privatisation officials would be completely powerless under an acting minister, he added.
Kaczmarek, known for his liberal views on privatisation, is a candidate for the treasury ministry of his ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party.
The smaller Polish Peasant Party (PSL) proposes its Planning Minister Miroslaw Pietrewicz for the post.
The two parties on Thursday apparently overcame a three-week-old deadlock in talks on the reshuffle and decided to meet later this week to discuss the appointment.

Kaczmarek said he was ready to take over the treasury portfolio but stressed that appointing a Peasant official to head the ministry need not necessarily mean a privatisation slow-down, as many analysts fear.
"We should not base our judgement of the whole PSL on some of its members who oppose privatisation," said Kaczmarek.
Many Peasant deputies are against privatisation, notably involving foreign capital, and have repeatedly tried to remove Kaczmarek since the coalition government was created in 1993.

The treasury ministry, whose creation will start a cabinet reorganisation involoving the liquidation of seven ministries and the setting up several new ones, will supervise several hundred of the largest state-owned firms, with some 3,000 smaller ones handed over to the local governors.
The ministry will take over companies now controlled by the ministries of finance, industry, telecommunications and others, in a move desigend to streamline economic decision-making.
Kaczmarek said the government would meet early next week to decide which companies would be handed over to the treasury ministry.
